messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 55-year-old African American man who has spent decades as a bomb disposal technician, a job that once made him proud of how steady he could remain in chaos. The event that broke that confidence happened during a hurricane response on the Gulf Coast, when he was deployed to help clear unstable structures after severe flooding. In the middle of a neighborhood already stripped apart by wind and water, he was working near a damaged house when part of the structure gave way without warning. People were shouting over the storm noise, someone yelled for everyone to move, and the crack of collapsing timber came with such force that for a moment it sounded to him like an explosion. He remembers dirty water, splintered boards, and the helplessness of not knowing whether more of the house was about to come down. What remains most vivid is the suddenness of it and the soundscape around it—loud crashes, raised voices, orders shouted across confusion.

In the months afterward, unpredictability became hard for him to tolerate. At work, if a situation changed suddenly or someone shouted across a room, he would feel himself clamp down internally and begin managing the distress any way he could. He started avoiding anything he thought might become stressful, passing off certain field tasks when he could, staying away from noisy briefings, and keeping himself constantly occupied with television, cleaning, or pointless jobs around the house so his mind would never settle. In the evenings he would eat far past hunger, describing it less as enjoyment than as a way to blunt the agitation after a day of bracing himself against sudden noises and abrupt demands.

Those same cues also set off reactions that felt to Kwame as if his body had stopped waiting for his mind. A slammed metal door at the depot, a supervisor barking an instruction, an unexpected change in a routine assignment could make him jolt, tense, and scan the area before he had even registered what he thought was happening. At times the response sharpened into brief flashback-like moments in which he felt transported back into that flooded street, as if the collapse were happening again. The triggers did not just frighten him in the present; they also tugged at the memory itself. A loud noise or somebody shouting could pull up fragments—the cracked beam, muddy water, the sense of impact—but as soon as more of it started to come, he would push it away before he could see the whole thing.

That pattern has left him with a memory that feels both intrusive and unfinished. He says he remembers pieces, never a complete sequence, and when those pieces break through he is flooded with intense rage—rage at the chaos, at the lack of warning, at how quickly control vanished. Because the memory comes in fragments, he remains on edge, convinced that danger can arrive before there is time to understand it. And because his body so often reacts as if he is under threat, the memory itself becomes harder to approach; he cuts it off midway, refusing to let it fully form because he expects the physical surge and anger that come with it.

Over time this has tightened into a daily pattern. The more often he has false alarms and those sudden bodily reactions, the more he organizes his life around preventing them. He avoids stressful situations, keeps his attention filled every waking hour, and eats to settle himself after episodes of alarm. Yet this way of coping has made him more sensitive to the very things he is trying to manage. Because he is constantly watching for abrupt changes, shouting and loud noises stand out immediately. Because he avoids ordinary stress, even minor unpredictability now feels potent. At work in the bomb squad environment—where sharp commands and sudden noises are part of the day—he has become quicker to flinch and quicker to interpret the atmosphere as dangerous, even when nothing is actually wrong.

His efforts to push the memories away have also made the triggers feel broader and less predictable. Since he never lets the memory run to completion, it returns as disconnected sensory pieces that seem to latch onto whatever resembles the original chaos: a raised voice in the garage, a crash from dropped equipment, a last-minute change in plans. Those moments can ignite his body before he has words for what is happening, and once that surge starts he may spend the rest of the day distracting himself and eating compulsively just to come back down.

Kwame finally agreed to seek help after his wife told him that home now feels organized around his nerves. He avoids family gatherings if children are loud, keeps the television on late into the night so his mind never goes quiet, and has become more distant whenever she asks what happened during the hurricane deployment. What frightens him most is that he no longer trusts his own reactions; he feels his body can declare an emergency at any moment, and he fears that if he ever lets himself remember the event fully, the rage and panic will overtake him. What he hopes for, cautiously, is to be able to hear a sudden noise or a shouted instruction without feeling as though the disaster has started all over again.
